January and February

Peak high season and arguably the most flawless weather of the year: dry, bright, breezy, and warm without being sweltering. This is when the island fills with sun-seekers escaping the northern winter, so flights and hotels are at their priciest and the high-rise strip along Palm Beach is busiest. This is also the heart of Aruba Carnival, the island's biggest cultural celebration: weeks of music, costumed parades, jump-ups, and street parties that build from early January and peak with the Grand Parade through Oranjestad and the Lighting Parade in San Nicolas in the days before Lent. The Grand Parade is held on the Sunday before Ash Wednesday. If you want the spectacle, color, and music, this is the window, just book accommodation well ahead, because Carnival weekends sell out.

March and April

Still firmly in the dry, reliable, high-season sweet spot, just after the Carnival peak. The weather stays gorgeous and dependable, with low rainfall and steady trade winds. April delivers spring-break and Easter visitors, keeping things lively before the high-season crowds start to thin. April is also the start of one of the best value windows of the year.

May and June

The smart traveler's window. The weather is still dry and gorgeous, the sea is warming up nicely, yet prices and crowds drop noticeably once the winter rush ends. You get near-peak conditions at shoulder-season rates, ideal for a relaxed beach trip to the low-rise calm of Eagle Beach, a sunset catamaran cruise, or a jeep safari through Arikok. If you want our single best all-round recommendation, this stretch is it.

July and August

Warm, dry, and busy in a different way: summer draws Dutch and family visitors, so Palm Beach and Noord feel lively, though volumes stay below the winter peak. The sea is at its warm best and the diving is superb.Prices generally stay below the deep-winter peak. Book early if you are traveling on fixed school-holiday dates.

September, October, and November

The quietest and cheapest stretch of the year, and the off-season elsewhere that Aruba quietly turns to its advantage. Humidity ticks up and you may catch a few more passing showers, mostly brief and overnight, with October and November the slightly wetter months. In return you get the lowest fares, the best room rates, and beaches like Baby Beach and Mangel Halto nearly to yourself. The sea is still warm and the calm leeward coast still delivers. It is the ideal time for unhurried days exploring Arikok National Park or the street art of San Nicolas without the crowds.

December

A month of two halves. Early December is still calm and good value, a sweet spot before the rush. From roughly mid-December the holiday high season kicks in hard, with Christmas and New Year prices among the steepest of the year and beaches at their fullest. December also brings the cherished Dande Festival, the Aruban New Year's tradition of roving musicians singing house-to-house blessings for the year ahead. If you want December sun without December prices, aim for the first two weeks.

Prices by season

Aruba's pricing follows the crowds, not the weather, which is exactly why timing pays off here.

  • High season (mid-December to mid-April): Highest flight and hotel prices, busiest beaches, best to book months ahead. The Christmas and New Year fortnight is the absolute peak.
  • Shoulder season (mid-April to August): Excellent value with near-peak weather. Our top pick for the price-to-conditions ratio.
  • Low season (September to November): The cheapest fares and rooms of the year, with the trade-off of slightly higher humidity and a few more showers.

One budget note that applies in any season: Aruba uses the Aruban florin (currency code AWG), pegged at roughly 1.79 to the US dollar. US dollars are accepted almost everywhere, though change often comes back in florins, so a small dollar buffer plus a card covers most situations comfortably. Note that Aruba is a constituent country of the Kingdom of the Netherlands, and drivers keep to the right.

Events and crowd timing

Three events are worth planning a whole trip around.

Carnival (building from early January and peaking with the Grand Parade in Oranjestad and the Lighting Parade in San Nicolas in the days before Lent) is the island's biggest cultural celebration: weeks of music, costumed parades, jump-ups, and street parties. The dates float with the calendar, so they usually land in February. Come for it deliberately and book early, because rooms vanish, or avoid the parade weekends if crowds are not your thing.

Aruba Hi-Winds (May 13–18, 2026) turns Fishermen's Huts into a windsurfing and kitesurfing arena with trade winds, a magnet for board-sports fans and a great spectacle even if you are only watching.

Outside those peaks, crowd levels track the price seasons described above. For the emptiest beaches and the calmest version of Savaneta and Santa Cruz, or a quiet morning watching the flamingos and herons at the Bubali Bird Sanctuary, aim for the September-to-November low season or a midweek visit in any month.

Matching the season to your trip

Because the weather is so consistent, almost everything runs year-round, but a few activities reward smart timing. Boat-based trips such as a sunset catamaran cruise or a snorkel and sail cruise are at their smoothest in the calmer, drier months from roughly December to June. Diving and snorkeling visibility is excellent all year but the water is warmest from July to October, ideal for the Antilla shipwreck dive. Hiking and four-wheeling through Arikok National Park to reach the Natural Pool is most comfortable in the cooler, drier early months, and always best started early before the desert heat builds. And a slow wander past the pastel Dutch facades of Oranjestad, a ride on the Oranjestad streetcar, and a climb up Casibari Rock Formations for the view of Hooiberg are a delight in any season.

The strongest winds generally arrive from May through July, with a calmer stretch from September through November. June is the windiest month (averaging about 20 mph), while November is the calmest (about 12.5 mph). Local schools consider December through August the most consistent stretch for kitesurfing. In the calmer window they report winds of roughly 10 to 18 knots and about a 60% chance of usable wind, so bring larger kites or foil boards.

The bottom line

If you want the most reliably perfect weather and do not mind paying for it, come December through April. If you want the best balance of great conditions and fair prices, come in April, May, or June. If you want the cheapest possible Caribbean escape with the trade-off of a little humidity, come September through November and let the rest of the hemisphere's hurricane season work in your favor. Whichever you choose, you are landing on a warm, dry, sunny desert island that delivers swimmable seas and clear leeward beaches every month of the calendar.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the cheapest time to visit Aruba?

September through November is the cheapest stretch, with the lowest flight and hotel prices of the year. The trade-off is slightly higher humidity and a few more passing showers, mostly brief and overnight, but the calm leeward beaches and warm sea stay fully usable.

Does Aruba get hurricanes?

Direct hurricane strikes are very rare. Aruba sits in the far southern Caribbean, off the coast of Venezuela, on the southern fringes of the Atlantic hurricane belt rather than outside it, so the island is not immune: passing tropical systems can cause beach erosion and coastal flooding. The island may occasionally feel the distant edge of a system as extra wind or swell, but wholesale wash-outs are not part of the normal pattern.

When is the water warmest in Aruba?

The sea is warmest from late summer into autumn, around 29C (84F), making July to October the favorite of many divers and snorkelers. That said, the water never really cools off, sitting around 26 to 27C (79 to 81F) even in the winter months, so swimming is comfortable in every season.

When is Aruba Carnival?

Carnival builds from early January with warm-up parties and jump-ups, then peaks with the Grand Parade through Oranjestad and the Lighting Parade in San Nicolas in the days leading up to Lent, with the Grand Parade held on the Sunday before Ash Wednesday. If you want to experience it, book accommodation well in advance, as Carnival weekends sell out.

What is the rainiest time in Aruba?

October through December is the slightly wetter stretch, with the most rain typically falling in late autumn. Even then, Aruba is a desert island, so rain usually comes as short overnight or early-morning showers rather than all-day downpours, and it rarely ruins a beach day.

What is the best month to visit Aruba overall?

For the best balance of weather and value, April through June is hard to beat: still dry and bright, with a warming sea, but at noticeably lower prices and with thinner crowds than the December-to-April high season. For the most flawless weather regardless of cost, the high-season months from December through April are the safest bet.

guides.title: Things to Do in Aruba
guides.summary: Things to do in Aruba: snorkel a shipwreck off Boca Catalina, jeep through Arikok National Park, and watch the sunset from a catamaran deck.
guides.html:
Aruba packs a remarkable amount into one small, sunny island. It is a constituent country of the Kingdom of the Netherlands, sitting just off the coast of Venezuela on the southern fringes of the hurricane belt, and the weather holds steady at around 28C (82F) with constant trade winds and very little rain. The calm leeward beaches on the west and southwest are made for swimming and snorkeling, while the wild windward northeast coast, with its cactus, divi-divi trees, and crashing surf, is made for adventure. This guide walks you through the experiences worth building a trip around, from floating over a shipwreck to watching the sun drop from the deck of a catamaran.

Everything here is easy to reach. Aruba calls itself One Happy Island, English and Spanish are spoken everywhere alongside the official Papiamento and Dutch, US dollars are accepted right alongside the Aruban florin, and you drive on the right. Start with the water, then head inland to the desert park, and finish with the island's culture in Oranjestad and San Nicolas.

Snorkel the calm leeward coast

The west coast is one of the easiest places in the Caribbean to step off the sand and straight onto living reef. The water is clear, the entries are gentle, and you rarely need a boat to find something worth the trip.

Boca Catalina and Malmok

Boca Catalina is the island's signature snorkel cove, a small sheltered bay north of Palm Beach where calm, shallow water is full of sergeant majors, parrotfish, and the odd ray. You can wade in from the rocky shore and stay close to the surface over the reef. Just south, Malmok Beach has more rocky reef along its edges and is a favorite launch point for boat snorkel trips. Bring water shoes for the rocky entries, and come in the morning before the afternoon breeze ruffles the surface. See our overview of snorkeling at Boca Catalina for guided and self-guided options.

The Antilla shipwreck

The Antilla is one of the largest wrecks in the Caribbean, a German freighter scuttled off the northwest coast during the Second World War. It rests in relatively shallow water near Malmok, encrusted in coral and swarming with fish, and the upper sections sit close enough to the surface that snorkelers can take it in from above while divers explore the holds. Most catamaran and boat tours include a stop here. If you want to go deeper, the Antilla shipwreck dive takes you right inside the structure. The whole reef system off this coast falls within the Aruba Marine Park, so the usual reef etiquette applies: look, do not touch.

More calm-water spots

  • Mangel Halto on the southeast coast is a mangrove-fringed cove with a reef channel that is excellent for both snorkeling and paddleboarding at Mangel Halto.
  • Arashi Beach at the northwest tip has calm, clear water and reef on its rocky flanks, near the California Lighthouse.
  • Tres Trapi, named for its three steps down to the sea, is a small local snorkel spot where green turtles are sometimes seen grazing.
  • Baby Beach at the island's southern tip is a shallow, calm lagoon, ideal for families and gentle first-time snorkeling.

Take a jeep safari through Arikok National Park

Arikok National Park covers nearly a fifth of Aruba, a rugged desert of cactus, volcanic hills, gold-mine ruins, and a dramatic windward coastline. A four-wheel-drive is the way to see it, because the interior tracks are rough and the best sights are spread out. A guided jeep safari through Arikok takes the hassle out of navigation and gets you to the highlights.

Inside and around the park, look for these landmarks:

  • The Natural Pool (Conchi), a sheltered rock-ringed basin on the wild coast where you can swim while waves break on the outer rocks. It is reachable only on foot, by horse, or by four-wheel-drive.
  • Dos Playa and Andicuri, two wild windward beaches with powerful surf, beautiful to see but not for swimming.
  • The Natural Bridge area on the north coast, where the sea has carved arches out of the limestone.
  • Caves with ancient rock drawings and stands of towering cactus that define the park's stark beauty.

Bring plenty of water, sun protection, and sturdy shoes. The park is hot and shadeless, and the trade winds can be deceptively strong on the exposed coast.

Explore the rock formations and lighthouse country

Away from the park, Aruba's dry interior hides a cluster of unusual sights. The Casibari rock formations and the nearby Ayo rock formations are giant tumbled boulders you can climb for views across the island, with Ayo also holding ancient Indigenous pictographs. Rising in the middle of the island is Hooiberg, a haystack-shaped hill with a long staircase to a panoramic summit.

At the northwest tip, the California Lighthouse stands over the windswept dunes and is a classic sunset perch. Not far away, the simple Alto Vista Chapel, the island's first church, sits alone on a cactus-covered hillside above the sea. A guided horseback riding tour is a memorable way to reach the chapel and the quieter stretches of the north coast.

Sail at sunset on a catamaran

An evening sail is one of Aruba's signature experiences. A sunset catamaran cruise glides along the calm leeward coast off Palm Beach and Eagle Beach as the sky turns gold, usually with drinks, music, and an easy, social atmosphere on deck. Daytime snorkel and sail cruises combine the sail with stops at the Antilla wreck and Boca Catalina, so you get both the reef and the ride in one trip.

For more time on the water, the island also offers parasailing over Palm Beach, deep-sea fishing charters, a submarine tour over the reefs, and a full day at De Palm Island, a private island set up for snorkeling, slides, and all-inclusive ease.

Catch the wind: windsurfing and kitesurfing

Aruba's relentless trade winds make it one of the best wind-sport destinations in the Caribbean. Windsurfing at Fishermans Huts (Hadicurari), just north of the high-rise hotels on Palm Beach, is the classic spot: steady side-shore wind, flat shallow water close to shore, and a friendly scene for beginners and freestylers alike. It hosts the long-running Aruba Hi-Winds event, held May 13 to 18 in 2026.

For stronger riders, kitesurfing at Boca Grandi on the windward southeast coast offers bigger wind and waves, suited to experienced kiters rather than first-timers. Lessons and rentals are available at Fishermans Huts if you want to learn the basics in calmer conditions first.

Wander Oranjestad, the capital

Oranjestad is a walkable, colorful capital of Dutch colonial facades painted in pastel. Hop on the free Oranjestad streetcar, a vintage trolley that loops through the main shopping streets, and stop at Fort Zoutman, the island's oldest building, which houses a small historical museum and hosts the weekly Bon Bini Festival of music, food, and dance. Stroll the green of Wilhelmina Park along the waterfront, browse the marina, and sample local dishes like keshi yena, pastechi, and pan bati, washed down with a cold Balashi beer or a signature Aruba Ariba cocktail.

Discover the street art of San Nicolas

San Nicolas, the island's second city in the south, has reinvented itself as Aruba's cultural capital. Once a sleepy refinery town, it is now covered in San Nicolas street art, with huge, vivid murals by international artists turning whole buildings into open-air galleries. The city hosts the annual Aruba Art Fair and is nicknamed Sunrise City. Nearby beaches like Rodgers Beach and Baby Beach make an easy add-on to a mural-hunting afternoon.

See more of the island's nature

Aruba's wild side is not only in Arikok. The Bubali Bird Sanctuary near Palm Beach is a wetland that draws herons, egrets, and migratory birds to its former salt pans, with a watchtower for viewing. The mangroves and inlets of Spanish Lagoon shelter a mangrove forest and plenty of birdlife. Animal lovers can also visit the donkey and butterfly attractions for a gentler outing with children. For the full sweep of beaches, from the famous Eagle Beach with its wind-bent fofoti trees to the quiet Druif Beach and Manchebo Beach, see our full list of Aruba beaches.

Time it with a festival

Aruba's calendar is full of color. Aruba Carnival runs through January and February with weeks of parades, music, and costumes, building to the grand finale before Lent. The Aruba Hi-Winds competition filled Fishermans Huts with sails from May 13 to 18 in 2026. At year's end, the Dande Festival ushers in the New Year with traditional song. Browse the full events calendar to plan around them.

A simple first-timer plan

To string it together: spend your first morning snorkeling at Boca Catalina and the Antilla wreck on a snorkel-and-sail cruise, then relax on Eagle Beach in the afternoon. Devote a full day to a jeep safari through Arikok, the Natural Pool, and the rock formations. Save an evening for a sunset catamaran sail off Palm Beach. Then give a half-day to culture, splitting it between the Oranjestad streetcar and the murals of San Nicolas. Rent a car or join tours, carry US dollars or florin for entry fees, and drink plenty of water in the desert heat.

Frequently Asked Questions

What are the must-do activities in Aruba?

The top experiences are snorkeling at Boca Catalina and the Antilla shipwreck, a four-wheel-drive jeep safari through Arikok National Park to the Natural Pool, a sunset catamaran cruise off Palm Beach, windsurfing at Fishermans Huts, and exploring the capital Oranjestad and the street art of San Nicolas. Most can be done off the beach or on an easy half-day tour.

Where is the best snorkeling in Aruba?

Boca Catalina is the most popular calm cove for shore snorkeling, with clear shallow water full of fish. The Antilla shipwreck near Malmok is a highlight for both snorkelers and divers. Mangel Halto, Arashi Beach, Tres Trapi, and Baby Beach are other gentle, calm-water spots on the leeward and southern coasts.

Do I need a four-wheel-drive to visit the Natural Pool?

Yes. The Natural Pool, known locally as Conchi, sits on the rugged windward coast inside Arikok National Park and is reachable only on foot, by horseback, or by four-wheel-drive. The easiest way to reach it is on a guided jeep safari, which handles the rough interior tracks for you.

When is the best time to go to Aruba?

Aruba is warm, dry, and sunny year-round at around 28C (82F), so any month works, though the island is on the southern fringes of the hurricane belt and a passing tropical system can bring rain. Trade winds keep it comfortable. Time a visit with Carnival in January and February or Aruba Hi-Winds (May 13 to 18 in 2026) if you want the island at its liveliest.

What is there to do in San Nicolas?

San Nicolas, Aruba's southern city, is the island's street-art capital, covered in large murals by international artists and home to the annual Aruba Art Fair. Combine a mural walk with a visit to the calm Baby Beach and Rodgers Beach nearby for an easy half-day away from the resort strip.

Can beginners try windsurfing or kitesurfing in Aruba?

Yes. Fishermans Huts, just north of Palm Beach, has steady side-shore wind and flat, shallow water that is ideal for learning to windsurf, with lessons and rentals on site. Kitesurfing at Boca Grandi on the windward coast has stronger wind and waves and is better suited to experienced riders.

destinations.name: Eagle Beach
destinations.tagline: Aruba's wide low-rise beach of divi-divi trees
destinations.summary: Eagle Beach is Aruba's broad, low-rise stretch of powder-soft sand, framed by the island's iconic windswept divi-divi trees. Spacious, calm and consistently rated among the world's best beaches.
destinations.html:
Eagle Beach is the wide, low-rise jewel of Aruba's leeward coast, a broad sweep of powder-soft white sand and calm turquoise water that is regularly named among the best beaches in the world. Set just south of the high-rise strip, it trades towers for a low-rise zone of smaller resorts, so the sand stays spacious and uncrowded even in high season. Its emblem is the pair of windswept divi-divi trees, bent permanently southwest by the constant trade winds, the most photographed image on the island.

Eagle Beach is the showpiece, a generous arc of fine sand with gently shelving, clear water that is excellent for swimming, with palapa shade huts spaced along the shore. The breadth of the beach gives it a relaxed, unhurried feel, and the sunsets here, framed by the leaning divi-divi trees, are the classic Aruba postcard. Just to the south, Manchebo Beach and Druif Beach continue the calm, low-rise mood.

Nearby

  • The Bubali Bird Sanctuary, a wetland alive with herons and egrets, sits just inland.
  • The quieter sands of Manchebo Beach and Druif Beach extend the low-rise strip to the south.
  • The bars, dining and watersports of Palm Beach are a short drive north when you want more action.

The appeal of Eagle Beach is space and calm. You come here for room to spread out, gentle swimming and that quintessential divi-divi sunset, rather than for nightlife or a dense resort scene. It still has comfortable hotels, beach bars and watersports, but at a lower-key pace than the high-rise strip.

As a base, Eagle Beach suits couples and families who want a beautiful beach without the crowds, within an easy drive of both the dining and casinos of Palm Beach and the culture of Oranjestad. Horseback riding is prohibited on Aruba's beaches.

destinations.name: Noord
destinations.tagline: Aruba's northwest district of resorts, chapels and lighthouses
destinations.summary: Noord is the bustling northwest district behind the resort beaches, home to Alto Vista Chapel, the California Lighthouse, dining and nightlife, and the gateway to the quiet northern coves.
destinations.html:
Noord is the large district that spreads across the northwest of Aruba, the busy hinterland behind the resort beaches and the gateway to the island's far northern tip. More residential and varied than the beach strip, it bundles together dining, nightlife, churches and historic landmarks with easy access to a string of quiet leeward coves. For travellers who want to stay near the action of Palm Beach yet explore beyond it, Noord is the practical hub.

Two landmarks define the district. The California Lighthouse stands on the windswept northern point, named for a steamship wrecked offshore, with sweeping views over the dunes and both coastlines from its base. Inland, the simple yellow Alto Vista Chapel, the island's first church, sits alone on a cactus hillside above the sea, reached by a pilgrimage road lined with white crosses.

Quiet coves and reefs

  • Arashi Beach is a calm, sandy local favourite near the lighthouse, good for swimming and easy snorkeling.
  • Boca Catalina and Malmok Beach are rocky-edged coves with clear water and some of the island's best shore snorkeling.
  • The huge Antilla shipwreck lies just off the Malmok coast, a highlight for divers and snorkel-sail trips.

Noord covers a lot of ground, so it rewards a rental car. Beyond the resorts you will find local restaurants, supermarkets and the island's densest cluster of nightlife away from the beach itself. The northern coast around the lighthouse is windier and more rugged, with dunes and rocky shores, while the southwest-facing coves stay calm and swimmable.

The district pairs naturally with the resort beaches it backs onto and with day trips north to the lighthouse and the snorkel coves. Most visitors base themselves near Palm Beach within Noord or nearby Eagle Beach in Oranjestad West and head out from there for chapels, sunsets and the quiet northern sand.

photo.credit: Natalie Liao Jen via Wikimedia Commons

destinations.name: Oranjestad
destinations.tagline: Aruba's pastel Dutch capital of forts, trams and street art
destinations.summary: Oranjestad pairs Dutch colonial facades, the free streetcar and Fort Zoutman with cruise-port shopping and harbour dining. The island's culture, history and capital base.
destinations.html:
Oranjestad is the capital of Aruba and the cultural heart of the island, a compact harbour city built around a cruise port and a grid of Dutch colonial streets. Named for the Dutch House of Orange, it wears its heritage in candy-coloured facades, gabled rooftops and shaded plazas, a small-scale echo of the Netherlands set against a desert backdrop of cactus and constant trade winds. For a first visit it makes the natural base, central, walkable and close to the resort beaches of Palm Beach and Eagle Beach just up the coast.

The signature landmark is Fort Zoutman, the island's oldest building, whose Willem III Tower once doubled as a lighthouse and town clock and now houses the Historical Museum. Nearby, the leafy Wilhelmina Park runs along the marina, while the free Oranjestad streetcar trundles a loop through downtown, an open-sided tram that is the easiest way to see the centre. Main Street and the harbourfront malls draw cruise-day shoppers for jewellery, liqueur and souvenirs.

What to do

  • Tour Fort Zoutman and the Historical Museum, then stroll Wilhelmina Park by the marina.
  • Ride the free Oranjestad streetcar on its downtown loop past the pastel facades.
  • Sample island flavours, from keshi yena to a fresh pastechi, at harbour cafes and the local market.
  • Time a visit for the weekly Bon Bini Festival at the fort, an evening of music, dance and food.

By day the city is for wandering, shopping and history; the wider downtown also serves as the launch point for the island's sailing and dive trips, though Red Sail and De Palm sunset catamaran cruises depart from Palm Beach. Papiamento is the language of the street, but Dutch, English and Spanish are all widely spoken, so ordering food and asking directions is easy.

Oranjestad puts you within a short drive of both the high-rise resort strip to the north and the wild windward interior of Arikok National Park to the east. Use it for culture, dining and convenience, then drive out to the sand and the desert.

photo.alt: Plaza Daniel Leo in Oranjestad, Aruba

destinations.name: Palm Beach
destinations.tagline: Aruba's high-rise resort strip and watersports hub
destinations.summary: Palm Beach is Aruba's liveliest resort strip: a calm white-sand bay backed by high-rise hotels, beach bars and watersports, with restaurants, a pier and nightlife steps from the sand.
destinations.html:
Palm Beach is the resort and watersports heart of Aruba, a long ribbon of soft white sand on the calm leeward northwest coast, backed by the island's high-rise hotels. This is the corner built for an easy, full-service beach holiday: gentle, clear water, rows of palapa shade huts, beach bars, piers and a non-stop parade of watersports. For travellers who want sand, sun-loungers, dining, casinos and nightlife all within walking distance, this is the most convenient stretch of the island.

Palm Beach itself is the centrepiece, a wide, sheltered bay where the water stays calm and shallow near shore, ideal for swimming, paddleboarding and easy snorkeling. Just offshore lie the Fishermans Huts flats, one of the Caribbean's classic windsurfing and kitesurfing spots thanks to the steady trade winds. Behind the sand, the high-rise strip packs in the island's densest cluster of restaurants, bars, shops and casinos.

On the water

  • Book a parasailing flight or a sunset catamaran cruise straight off the beach.
  • Dive or snorkel the Antilla shipwreck, a huge WWII wreck a short boat ride offshore.
  • Windsurf or kitesurf the flats at the Fishermans Huts at the quieter north end.

The trade-off for all this convenience is that Palm Beach is the busiest, most developed part of Aruba. You come here for comfort, action and a full-service beach day, not for solitude. When you want a calmer, lower-rise scene, the wide sands and fofoti trees of Eagle Beach are minutes south, while the dining and resorts of the Noord district sit just inland.

Because so much is concentrated here, Palm Beach works well for families who want safe swimming and amenities, and for couples and groups who like a beach by day and a casino or bar by night. A rental car is useful for exploring, but you can have a relaxed stay barely leaving the bay.

photo.alt: Palm Beach, Aruba, seen from a hotel pier
photo.credit: Bjørn Christian Tørrissen via Wikimedia Commons

destinations.name: San Nicolas
destinations.tagline: Aruba's Sunrise City of murals, music and Baby Beach
destinations.summary: San Nicolas, Aruba's second city, is the colourful Sunrise City: a sprawling open-air street-art gallery, lively local culture, and the calm shallow lagoon of Baby Beach nearby.
destinations.html:
San Nicolas is Aruba's second city and the cultural counterpoint to the resort strip, an old oil-refinery town on the southeast coast reborn as the island's arts capital. Nicknamed Sunrise City, it has transformed its weathered streets into a sprawling open-air gallery of bold, large-scale murals, with new works added each year. More gritty and authentically local than the beach strip, it offers a window into everyday Aruban life, layered with Caribbean migration, music and food.

The draw is the San Nicolas street art, dozens of vivid murals splashed across building walls throughout downtown, best explored on foot or a guided walking tour. The city has a strong music and carnival tradition, hosts the annual Aruba Art Fair, and keeps a lively bar and local-dining scene around its main street. It feels a world away from the polished northwest, in the best sense.

Beaches and nearby

  • Baby Beach, a shallow, sheltered lagoon near the southern tip, is the island's calmest swimming spot, ideal for families and beginner snorkelers.
  • Rodgers Beach sits just around the point, a quiet local cove with clear water.
  • The wind-battered southeast point at Boca Grandi is a kitesurfing hotspot, though its surf is too rough for swimming.

San Nicolas covers a wide area, so a rental car helps for combining the murals downtown with the beaches at the southern tip. The contrast is part of the appeal: a working town with real character one moment, the glass-clear lagoon of Baby Beach the next. Sample local flavours here too, from a hearty kabritu stoba to a cold Balashi beer.

The city pairs with the calm southern beaches and the southeast coast's wild kitesurfing waters. Many visitors come on a day trip from the resort areas, about a 30 to 40 minute drive from Oranjestad, but San Nicolas rewards a slower look at the island's creative, lived-in side.

destinations.name: Santa Cruz
destinations.tagline: Aruba's green heart, Hooiberg and Arikok gateway
destinations.summary: Santa Cruz is Aruba's central inland district: the island's agricultural heart, home to the Hooiberg landmark hill and the rock formations and trails of nearby Arikok National Park.
destinations.html:
Santa Cruz is the inland district at the green heart of Aruba, a spread-out farming and residential community in the island's centre. Far from the beaches and the cruise port, it is the most authentically local part of the island, a landscape of cunucu (countryside) homesteads, cactus, aloe fields and goats. For travellers curious about the real, lived-in Aruba and its dramatic desert interior, Santa Cruz is the launch point.

Rising above the district is the Hooiberg, the haystack-shaped hill that is one of the island's most recognisable landmarks. A long flight of concrete steps climbs to the top, where on a clear day you can see across the whole island and even glimpse Venezuela on the horizon. Nearby stand the giant boulders of the Casibari and Ayo rock formations, mysterious tumbled monoliths with footpaths, ancient petroglyphs and viewpoints.

The wild interior

  • Climb the steps up the Hooiberg for the island's best all-round panorama.
  • Scramble the Casibari and Ayo boulder formations, dotted with paths and petroglyphs.
  • Enter Arikok National Park, which covers nearly a fifth of the island, on a jeep safari to the Natural Pool, caves and wild windward coast.

Santa Cruz is the doorway to Arikok National Park, the rugged protected wilderness that fills the island's east. Within it lie the Natural Pool (Conchi), a sea-carved rock basin reached only by 4x4, horseback or a long hike, the limestone caves, and the surf-battered Atlantic coast where windward beaches like Dos Playa are stunning but far too rough for swimming.

This is a district for adventure and scenery rather than beach lounging. A rental car or guided tour is convenient, as the interior is dry, hilly and lightly serviced. Santa Cruz sits central, roughly 20 minutes from Oranjestad, making it the natural base for exploring Aruba's wild side.

photo.alt: Cas Sour Judith in Santa Cruz, Aruba

destinations.name: Savaneta
destinations.tagline: Aruba's oldest village, fishing roots and the Mangel Halto reef
destinations.summary: Savaneta is Aruba's original capital and oldest village, a low-key fishing community on the south coast known for fresh seafood and the mangrove-fringed snorkel reef at Mangel Halto.
destinations.html:
Savaneta is the oldest village on Aruba and the island's first capital, a quiet, strung-out fishing community along the calm south-central coast. Long before the resorts, this was the island's main settlement, and it keeps a slow, lived-in feel: cunucu (countryside) houses, small fishing boats, and one of the island's best collections of seafood restaurants, several built right over the water. For travellers who want an authentic, unhurried slice of Aruba away from the crowds, Savaneta delivers.

The natural highlight is Mangel Halto, a sheltered, mangrove-fringed cove with a shallow turquoise lagoon and a reef that drops off just beyond, making it one of the island's premier shore-snorkel and dive sites. The calm inner lagoon is perfect for beginners and paddleboarding, while the deeper outer reef rewards confident snorkelers and divers with coral, fish and good visibility.

What to do

  • Snorkel or dive the reef at Mangel Halto, then paddle the calm mangrove lagoon.
  • Eat fresh catch of the day at the village's waterfront seafood spots.
  • Explore the nearby Spanish Lagoon, a Ramsar-listed wetland and the island's main mangrove habitat.

Savaneta is a place to slow down rather than a resort hub, with limited accommodation and a handful of standout restaurants rather than nightlife. The south coast here is calm and swimmable, sheltered by reefs and mangroves, a contrast to the wild windward shore on the other side of the island. A rental car is useful, as sights are spread along the coastal road.

The village pairs naturally with the snorkel reefs of the south coast and the wetlands of Spanish Lagoon, and sits roughly midway between Oranjestad and the murals of San Nicolas, making it an easy stop on a drive along the southern coast.

beaches.name: Andicuri Beach
beaches.tagline: A remote windward bay, not for swimming
beaches.summary: A remote, photogenic bay on the wild windward coast, framed by rocky cliffs and crashing surf, popular for dramatic scenery and bodyboarding but unsafe for swimming.
beaches.html:
Andicuri is a remote, strikingly beautiful bay on Aruba's wild northeast (windward) coast, reached by rough tracks through the island's rugged interior. A wide crescent of golden sand is hemmed by rocky cliffs and battered by Atlantic surf, a raw and scenic spot that draws photographers, adventurers and experienced bodyboarders rather than sunbathers.

Like the rest of the windward coast, Andicuri is exposed to strong trade winds, powerful waves and dangerous currents, so it is not a safe swimming beach. Confident bodyboarders and surfers sometimes ride the breaks here, but most visitors come for the dramatic landscape, the sea spray against the cliffs and the sense of wild isolation. Until it collapsed, Aruba's famous Natural Bridge stood just up the coast from here.

Important to know

  • There is strong surf; experienced swimmers can enter the water, yet must be aware of currents.
  • Access is over rough tracks; a four-wheel-drive vehicle is recommended.
  • There are no facilities or lifeguards, and only a little shade from the cliffs, so bring everything you need.
  • Come for the scenery, photography and the wild windward coast.

Andicuri sits on the windward coast in the Santa Cruz interior near the Natural Bridge and the wild bays of Dos Playa. A guided jeep safari or ATV tour is the easiest way to reach this rugged coastline.

beaches.name: Arashi Beach
beaches.tagline: Calm snorkeling cove near the lighthouse
beaches.summary: A calm, white-sand cove near the island's northwestern tip, popular for easy snorkeling over a shallow reef and for sunsets beneath the nearby California Lighthouse.
beaches.html:
Arashi Beach sits near the northwestern tip of Aruba, the last of the calm leeward beaches before the wild windward coast begins. It is a relaxed cove of soft white sand and clear, shallow turquoise water, quieter and more natural than the resort beaches further south. The gentle entry makes it good for swimming, and a rocky reef on the left side of the beach when facing the sea draws snorkelers.

The reef just offshore holds reef fish and is easy to reach straight from the sand, making Arashi one of the better shore-snorkel spots on the calm coast. A few palapas dot the beach for shade, and Arashi Beach Shack serves food and drinks, but it stays low-key. Its position near the California Lighthouse makes it a popular stop for sunset, when the light over the water and the dunes turns golden.

Visiting Arashi

  • Entry is free with a parking area behind the beach.
  • Bring snorkel gear to explore the reef on the left side of the beach when facing the sea.
  • A few palapas provide shade; arrive early to claim one.
  • Stay for sunset near the California Lighthouse for the best light.

Arashi sits in the Noord district near the snorkeling coves of Boca Catalina and Malmok Beach, all within a short drive. Combine a snorkel here with the California Lighthouse and a sunset over the northwestern point.

beaches.name: Baby Beach
beaches.tagline: A calm lagoon ideal for families with small kids
beaches.summary: A shallow, near-enclosed lagoon at Aruba's southeastern tip, with bath-warm, knee-deep water that makes it ideal for families with small kids.
beaches.html:
Baby Beach sits at the far southeastern end of Aruba, near the town of San Nicolas, and is named for its shallow, gentle water. A constructed barrier almost encloses the bay, creating a calm, crescent-shaped lagoon where the water stays warm and shallow well out from shore. That makes it ideal for families with small kids.

The protected lagoon is also a friendly place to learn to snorkel: reef fish gather near the rocky edges of the bay, and the calm water means easy, low-stress entries. Where the lagoon opens out to the sea, snorkelers should watch out for strong currents; for your safety, stay within the marked snorkel area. Snack bars operate behind the sand, with complimentary huts and cabana rentals on the beach, and a casual beach restaurant nearby is a local favourite.

Visiting Baby Beach

  • Entry is free with a parking area behind the beach.
  • Bring or rent snorkel gear to explore the reef fish near the rocky edges.
  • Stay inside the lagoon, and within the marked snorkel area when snorkeling; the open water beyond the rock barrier has strong current and is not for swimming.
  • Complimentary huts and a snack bar provide shade and food, but bring water and sun protection.

Baby Beach is the highlight of the San Nicolas area, close to the snorkeling at Rodgers Beach and the colourful San Nicolas street art in town. Combine a morning swim here with a stroll through the murals of Aruba's Sunrise City.

beaches.name: Boca Catalina
beaches.summary: A tiny, sheltered snorkeling cove on the calm northwest coast, with clear shallow water full of reef fish and an easy entry that suits beginners and families alike.
beaches.html:
Boca Catalina is a small, sheltered cove on Aruba's calm northwest coast that has become one of the island's best-loved shore-snorkeling spots. The compact crescent of pale sand drops into clear, shallow water where schools of reef fish gather close to shore, so you barely have to swim out to be surrounded by them. The calm, protected conditions make it ideal for beginners and families.

Because the snorkeling is so good and so easy, snorkel-and-sail boat tours often stop here, and the cove can get busy at midday. Early morning is the calmest and least crowded time, with the best visibility. There are some makeshift beach huts for shade, so come prepared. The rocky edges of the bay shelter the fish and keep the water still.

Snorkel tips for Boca Catalina

  • Bring your own snorkel gear; there are no rentals at the cove.
  • Arrive early to beat the boat tours and find a spot on the small beach.
  • Stay near the rocky edges where the reef fish gather.
  • There is little shade and no lifeguard, so pack sun protection and water.

Boca Catalina sits in the Noord district between Malmok Beach and Arashi Beach, all calm snorkeling coves within a short drive. A guided Boca Catalina snorkel trip often pairs the cove with the nearby Antilla shipwreck.

beaches.name: Dos Playa
beaches.tagline: Wild windward bays, not for swimming
beaches.summary: Two wild, dramatic sandy bays on the rugged windward coast inside Arikok National Park, framed by cliffs and pounding surf, stunning to see but not safe for swimming.
beaches.html:
Dos Playa is a pair of wild, scenic sandy bays on Aruba's rugged northeast (windward) coast, set inside Arikok National Park. Cliffs and rocky headlands frame two crescents of white sand pounded by Atlantic surf, a raw, untamed landscape that feels worlds away from the calm resort beaches on the leeward side. It is one of the most photographed wild spots on the island.

This is a place to admire rather than swim. The windward coast takes the full force of the trade winds and surf, producing strong waves, powerful currents and undertow that make swimming dangerous. Experienced surfers occasionally ride the breaks, but for most visitors Dos Playa is about the dramatic scenery, the empty sand and the wild coastline. Dos Playa is accessible by car or on foot.

Important to know

  • Swimming is not safe here: strong surf, current and undertow make the water dangerous.
  • Access is by car or on foot inside Arikok National Park; park fees apply.
  • There are no facilities or lifeguards, though sea-grape trees offer shade, so bring everything you need.
  • Come for the scenery, photography and the wild, empty coastline.

Dos Playa lies within Arikok National Park in the Santa Cruz interior, near the wild Andicuri Beach and the Natural Bridge. A guided Arikok jeep safari is the easiest way to see this rugged coast safely.

facts.label: Access
facts.value: Access by car or on foot

beaches.name: Druif Beach
beaches.summary: A relaxed, family-friendly stretch of soft white sand and calm clear water at the southern end of the low-rise strip, quieter than its famous neighbours but just as pretty.
beaches.html:
Druif Beach is a calm, easygoing stretch of fine white sand at the southern end of Aruba's low-rise coast, just below Manchebo. It carries the same powder sand and clear turquoise water as its more famous neighbours but with a quieter, more local feel. The relatively calm water suits swimming.

A handful of low-rise resorts back the beach, providing palapas, loungers and beach bars, but the mood stays relaxed. Calm water, soft sand and easy facilities make Druif a comfortable spot to settle in for the day without the crowds of the resort strip. The trade winds keep the air pleasant, and the western exposure gives lovely sunset light.

Practical notes

  • Entry is free with parking near the resorts behind the sand.
  • Palapas, loungers and a beach bar are available through the resorts.
  • The calm, shallow water suits families and casual swimmers.
  • Bring sun protection; natural shade is limited.

Druif sits in the Eagle Beach low-rise area, flowing north into Manchebo Beach and Eagle Beach, with the busier Palm Beach a short drive up the coast. The three southern beaches make an easy, quiet alternative to the resort strip.

beaches.name: Eagle Beach
beaches.summary: Aruba's most celebrated stretch of powder-white sand, famous for its wide-open space, gentle turquoise water and the two windswept fofoti trees that have become the island's signature postcard.
beaches.html:
Eagle Beach is the beach most people picture when they imagine Aruba: a broad, brilliant-white ribbon of soft sand backed by sea-grape bushes and the island's famous wind-bent fofoti trees. Regularly ranked among the best beaches in the world, it is wider and far less built-up than the high-rise strip to the north, with low-rise hotels set back from the sand and plenty of open space to spread out.

The water is calm, warm and shallow for a long way out, shading from clear aqua near the shore to deep turquoise further out. Constant trade winds keep the air comfortable even at midday, and the gentle entry makes it ideal for families, swimmers and anyone who just wants to float. The two leaning fofoti trees on Eagle Beach are the most photographed spot on Eagle Beach, framing the classic Aruba sunset shot.

What to know before you go

  • Entry is free and there is public parking along the road behind the sand.
  • Natural shade is limited, so bring an umbrella or rent a palapa where available.
  • Beach bars and food trucks operate along the back of the beach.
  • There are no full-time lifeguards, but the water is calm and family friendly.

Eagle Beach sits just south of the resort strip, an easy hop from Palm Beach and the quieter, low-key Manchebo Beach and Druif Beach next door. A sunset catamaran cruise is a popular way to end an Eagle Beach day. Come early for the calmest water and the best stretch of empty sand.

beaches.name: Malmok Beach
beaches.summary: A rocky-edged stretch on the calm northwest coast, prized as a snorkeling and windsurfing base and for its proximity to the Antilla shipwreck offshore.
beaches.html:
Malmok Beach is a narrow, rocky-edged stretch on Aruba's calm northwest coast, set among low-rise villas just south of Arashi. It is less a sunbathing beach than a snorkeling and watersports base: the clear, calm water and shallow reef close to shore make for excellent snorkeling, and the steady trade winds make this one of the island's classic windsurfing spots.

The biggest draw offshore is the Antilla shipwreck, a large World War II German freighter resting in shallow water nearby and one of the largest wrecks in the Caribbean. Snorkel and dive boats launch from this coast to reach it, and the reef closer in holds plenty of fish for an easy shore snorkel. The shoreline is rocky in places, so water shoes help.

Good to know

  • Entry is free with roadside parking near the villas.
  • Bring water shoes; the entry is rocky rather than soft sand.
  • Mornings bring the calmest water and the best snorkel visibility.
  • Windsurfers favour this coast for the steady trade winds.

Malmok sits in the Noord district south of Boca Catalina and Arashi Beach. Boats for the wreck dive depart from Palm Beach.

photo.alt: Windswept divi-divi tree at Malmok Beach, Aruba

beaches.name: Manchebo Beach
beaches.tagline: Aruba's widest beach, with a tranquil atmosphere
beaches.summary: The widest, most tranquil stretch of Aruba's low-rise coast, a vast sweep of soft sand prized for its calm, low-key atmosphere and gentle, uncrowded swimming.
beaches.html:
Manchebo Beach is the broadest and most peaceful section of Aruba's low-rise coast, an enormous sweep of fine white sand that flows south from Eagle Beach. Where Palm Beach is busy and developed, Manchebo is calm and uncrowded, with low-rise resorts set well back and acres of open sand to yourself. It is a favourite for quiet sunbathing, long walks and unhurried swims.

Currents converge here and the surf can be rough, so check conditions before swimming. Steady trade winds make this stretch a longtime base for windsurfers and for sunrise yoga sessions on the sand. Because of its width and tranquil mood, Manchebo also draws those looking for a more low-key, wellness-oriented beach day than the resort strip offers.

Good to know

  • Entry is free with parking near the low-rise resorts.
  • Shade is limited, so bring an umbrella; ask before using hotel palapas.
  • The wide, calm sand is ideal for walking, yoga and quiet swimming.
  • Beach restaurants nearby serve local food and sunset drinks.

Manchebo sits between Eagle Beach and Druif Beach in the Eagle Beach area, so the three flow into one another along the low-rise coast. Pair a quiet morning here with the livelier scene up at Palm Beach.

beaches.name: Mangel Halto
beaches.summary: A hidden mangrove-fringed cove on the southeast coast, with a maze of shallow turquoise channels, a long reef and some of the best, most varied snorkeling on the island.
beaches.html:
Mangel Halto is a quiet, mangrove-fringed cove on Aruba's southeast coast that many visitors miss, which is part of its charm. Small wooden decks and palapas perch over a maze of shallow, glassy turquoise channels that wind between the mangroves, and a long reef runs offshore. The combination of calm protected shallows and a healthy reef just beyond makes this one of the island's richest snorkeling spots.

Beginners can drift in the sheltered inner channels among small fish, while stronger snorkelers and divers head out to the reef wall, which drops away with coral, fish and good visibility. The setting is natural and peaceful, with picnic palapas under the trees and very little development. The water is exceptionally clear and the mood relaxed.

Snorkel tips for Mangel Halto

  • Entry is free with parking near the palapas above the cove.
  • Beginners should stay in the calm inner channels; the outer reef is for stronger swimmers.
  • Bring your own snorkel gear and water shoes for the rocky and mangrove edges.
  • Mornings bring the calmest, clearest water.

Mangel Halto sits in the Savaneta area on the southeast coast, a good base for paddleboarding through the mangroves. Combine it with the shallow lagoon at Baby Beach further southeast for a full day on the quieter coast.

beaches.name: Palm Beach
beaches.summary: Aruba's lively high-rise strip, a two-mile-long ribbon of white sand lined with resorts, palapas, watersports and beach bars, where the action runs from morning swims to sunset cocktails.
beaches.html:
Palm Beach is the energetic heart of Aruba's tourism. This long, palm-dotted stretch of soft white sand runs in front of the island's high-rise hotels, casinos and beach clubs, and it buzzes from morning to night. The water is calm, clear and shallow, with rows of thatched palapas, watersports stands, floating docks and beach bars lining the shore.

Because it is so well served, Palm Beach suits visitors who want everything within reach: jet skis, banana boats, parasailing, paddleboards, snorkel trips and sunset sails are available here. The De Palm sunset sail departs from De Palm Pier. The calm, protected water is excellent for swimming, and the northern end near the pier is a good spot to watch boats come and go. By night the boulevard behind the beach fills with restaurants, bars and live music.

Planning a Palm Beach day

  • Public access is free; palapas in front of hotels may be reserved for guests, but plenty of open sand remains.
  • Watersports operators line the beach for jet skis, parasailing and boat tours.
  • It is busiest midday and at sunset; mornings are calmer for swimming.
  • The boulevard behind the beach has shops, restaurants and bars.

Palm Beach sits in the resort district of Palm Beach, next to the calmer Eagle Beach and a short drive from the snorkeling coves at Malmok Beach and Boca Catalina. The Antilla shipwreck off this coast is a favourite for snorkel and dive trips.

beaches.name: Rodgers Beach
beaches.tagline: A quiet sheltered cove by Baby Beach
beaches.summary: A calm, sheltered cove next to Baby Beach at the island's southern tip, with soft sand, clear water and easy snorkeling, far quieter than the famous beaches up north.
beaches.html:
Rodgers Beach is a calm, sheltered cove tucked beside Baby Beach near the southern tip of Aruba, close to the town of San Nicolas. A gentle crescent of soft sand backs onto clear, shallow water that is protected by the surrounding coastline, making it an easy, quiet swimming and snorkeling beach well away from the busy resort strip.

The calm water and reef toward the edges of the bay make for relaxed snorkeling, and the beach is rarely crowded. An old refinery sits on the headland nearby, but the cove itself is pretty and peaceful, with palapas for shade and a nearby bar. Its position next to Baby Beach makes it easy to see both in one trip to the south of the island.

Good to know

  • Entry is free with parking behind the beach.
  • Bring snorkel gear to explore the reef toward the edges of the bay.
  • Palapas and a nearby bar provide shade and refreshments.
  • The calm, sheltered water suits families and easy swimming.

Rodgers Beach sits in the San Nicolas area beside Baby Beach, so the two pair naturally for a day in the south. Round it out with the murals of the San Nicolas street art in nearby Sunrise City.

beaches.name: Surfside Beach
beaches.tagline: The handy beach by the capital
beaches.summary: The most convenient beach right by Oranjestad and the airport, a calm, sandy stretch with a beach bar, easy swimming and quick access to the capital's shops and dining.
beaches.html:
Surfside Beach is the closest beach to Aruba's capital, sitting in Oranjestad and near the Queen Beatrix International Airport. Despite the name, the water here is calm and sheltered, with soft sand and an easy, shallow entry that makes it a handy swimming spot for those staying in town or with only a short time on the island.

The beach is well served, with a popular beach bar and restaurant, palapas and easy parking, and it draws a relaxed mix of locals and visitors. Its convenience is the main appeal: you can swim, grab lunch and still be minutes from the shops, casinos and waterfront of Oranjestad. It is a good first or last stop near the airport, and the western exposure gives nice sunsets over the water.

Good to know

  • Entry is free with parking near the beach bar.
  • A beach bar and restaurant serve food and drinks on site.
  • The calm, shallow water suits families and casual swimmers.
  • Planes pass overhead on approach to the nearby airport.

Surfside sits beside Oranjestad, an easy stop between the airport and the capital's sights such as Fort Zoutman, Wilhelmina Park and the Oranjestad streetcar. Combine a quick swim here with a stroll through the colourful capital.

beaches.name: Tres Trapi
beaches.tagline: Snorkel with sea turtles off the steps
beaches.summary: A small rocky cove named for its three steps down to the water, beloved as a snorkeling spot where sea turtles graze in clear, calm shallows on the northwest coast.
beaches.html:
Tres Trapi, which means three steps in Papiamento, is a small, rocky cove on Aruba's calm northwest coast named for the short flight of concrete steps that lead down into the water. It has little sand, but what it lacks as a sunbathing beach it makes up for underwater: the clear, calm shallows here are one of the most reliable places on the island to snorkel with green sea turtles.

Turtles graze on the seagrass beds just off the steps, and snorkelers often spot several in a single visit, along with rays and reef fish. The water is calm and sheltered, with an easy entry down the steps, though water shoes help on the rocky shoreline. It is a local favourite and stays relatively low-key, with no facilities on site.

Snorkel responsibly

  • Keep your distance from the turtles, never touch or chase them, and let them surface to breathe.
  • Bring your own snorkel gear and water shoes; there are no rentals or facilities.
  • Use the steps for an easy entry, and mornings for the calmest, clearest water.
  • Parking is limited roadside, so arrive early.

Tres Trapi sits in the Noord district near the snorkeling coves of Malmok Beach and Boca Catalina. Pair a turtle snorkel here with the reef fish at Boca Catalina for an easy morning on the calm northwest coast.
